newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels advance on Kinshasa in talks run-up.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels advance on Kinshasa in talks run-up.

text.p: Zaire's rebels say they are marching on the capital Kinshasa again as political manoeuvring intensifies ahead of Wednesday's meeting between President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
On the humanitarian front, an aid mission to a rebel-held area of eastern Zaire said on Sunday it had discovered thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees, many on the verge of death.
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson, who helped bring Mobutu and Kabila together on May 4, said the jury was still out on Kabila's democratic credentials.

"It's very important that Zaire be managed and governed democratically, that he have market reforms, that he institute human rights processes, that he deal with the refugees," Richardson told U.S.-based CNN television.
"The jury is still out on Kabila," he said. "He needs a lot of seasoning in the democratic process."
Julian Fleet, a U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) official, said a U.N. mission found about 5,000 to 6,000 refugees near a village at kilometre 82 (50 miles) south of Kisangani.
"Many people have died there and many more are on the verge of death," he told reporters in Kisangani.

Earlier, Kabila's "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha told a news conference that the rebels were abandoning a pledge to South African President Nelson Mandela at the first face-to-face meeting on May 4 not to advance on the capital.
"We are now advancing and will continue to advance. We shall now talk and fight, and fight and talk," he said, accusing Mobutu of using the talks to buy time to strengthen his Kinshasa defences.
The rebels were last reported less than 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming capital of five million.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated the mineral-rich country at the heart of Africa for over three decades.
The rebels, who took up arms in October and control three quarters of Africa's third-largest country, insist that Mobutu step down immediately and hand power to Kabila.

Karaha said the rebels might pull out of the South African peace initiative if Roman Catholic Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo accepted the job of Speaker -- the constitutional successor to the president in the event of death or incapacity.
Mobutu supporters, who have a majority in the transitional parliament, voted on Saturday to give him back the job.
Fearing Monsengwo's popularity in the event of elections, they joined forces with supporters of radical opposition Etienne Tshisekedi in July 1995 to oust him.
Monsengwo is still popular in a country with a Roman Catholic majority. Tshisekedi supporters dismiss the archbishop of rebel-held Kisangani as "Mobutist".
They have vowed to call a stay-at-home protest on Wednesday if Monsengwo accepts the job.
